title: Your dashboard doesn't make decisions for you: how to turn metrics into product priorities
description: A dashboard doesn't decide for you. How to organize metrics into activity, outcome and guardrails, and turn them into questions and decisions.

related.title: Clint Acquire
related.body: In practice: a landing page and a conversational flow designed from the funnel and conversion metrics.

blocks.text: It's easy to open a dashboard and find dozens of numbers: sessions, CTR, conversion, cost per lead, activation, retention, churn and revenue.
The problem starts when the team tries to track everything without defining which decision each metric is supposed to help make.
A dashboard can be visually well organized and still not be very useful. A metric only gains value when it helps you understand a behavior, evaluate an outcome or choose an action.
Start with the decision
Before adding a chart, ask:

items: What decision do we need to make?
What behavior could explain the outcome?
Which metric can answer the question?
What action will we consider if the number goes up or down?

blocks.text: If the goal is to improve activation in a SaaS, landing page visits can be useful for acquisition, but they don't explain whether new users reach the first moment of value. For that, you may need to measure account creation, onboarding completion and use of the core feature.
The right metric depends on the question.
Separate activity, outcome and quality metrics
A useful structure can organize metrics into three groups:
what do people do? Examples: visits, clicks, form starts, use of a feature.
what does the product or business achieve? Examples: conversion, activation, revenue, retention and opportunities generated.
is the outcome coming with unwanted effects? Examples: invalid leads, cancellations, errors, complaints, time to complete a task or drop-off at critical steps.
These categories aren't a universal taxonomy, but they help keep a team from celebrating a rising metric without checking the effect on the rest of the journey.
Build a metric tree
A main metric rarely explains everything on its own.
Imagine the goal is to increase qualified opportunities generated by the landing page. A simple tree could connect:
Relevant traffic → Lead conversion → Qualification → Meeting → Opportunity
Each step has its own metrics and possible causes.

If relevant traffic grows but conversion drops, look into how well channel, promise and page line up. If conversion grows but qualification drops, look into the offer, the audience and the information you ask for. If leads are qualified but don't move on to a meeting, the problem may be in the sales process or in response time.
The tree helps turn a final metric into questions you can investigate.
Define guardrail metrics
Every optimization needs to consider possible side effects.

A change that increases form submissions can also increase spam. A more aggressive CTA can generate more clicks and more frustration. Simplifying onboarding can speed up sign-up but leave users without understanding how to use the product.
That's why you should define a main metric and guardrail metrics before shipping a change. You don't need a huge dashboard. Pick a few metrics that represent the relevant risks for that decision.
Watch out for averages that hide differences
An overall rate can hide very different experiences.

Total conversion can improve because a high-volume campaign brought in visitors with high intent, while the mobile experience got worse. Onboarding can look efficient for experienced users and still be hard for beginners.

Whenever it makes sense, analyze segments like channel, device, campaign, user type or journey step. Avoid segmenting endlessly until you find a favorable number. Segments need to answer clear hypotheses and have enough volume for reliable interpretation.
A useful dashboard ends in a decision
A good visualization isn't just for showing what happened. It helps you notice a change, understand its context and decide what to investigate.
For example:

cards.v: the drop started after a recent change and shows up mostly on mobile.
the new version made interacting with the fields harder on small screens.
reproduce the flow on mobile devices, watch sessions and test a fix.

data.close: The dashboard doesn't prove the hypothesis. It helps you decide where to look for evidence.

blocks.text: That's an important difference between reporting metrics and working in a data-driven way. The goal isn't to produce more charts. It's to shrink the distance between noticing a problem and making a well-founded decision.
